opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest surprise was how little glue I actually had to write. I came into it expecting to spend weeks wiring up integrations, writing wrappers for every device, figuring out all the APIs. Instead I mostly just pointed the agent at my home network and said, "go figure out what's on here." It scanned around, found the lights, the speakers, the thermostat, poked at the local endpoints, read whatever docs it could find, and within an hour or so it had basically reverse-engineered a working control layer for most of the house. That was a little bit of a "wait, what?" moment for me.

The second thing that surprised me is how much the interface changes once that works. I used to have, I don't know, six different apps on my phone for all these devices, each with its own login and its own weird UI. Now I just text Dobby, "it's bedtime," and it dims everything, turns off the music, locks up, and sets the temperature. These apps probably shouldn't exist in their current form. A lot of software is going to end up as an API surface that agents talk to, and the human-facing UI becomes a single conversation.

And then the slightly uncomfortable surprise: it's very capable, and I gave it a lot of access pretty casually. You realize how much of your environment is just sitting there on the network, unauthenticated, and an agent will happily find and use all of it. So there's a real lesson about permissions and sandboxing. The capability arrived faster than the safety rails. It's magical, but you want to be thoughtful about what you're handing over the keys to.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker pointed Dobby at the home network and told it to “go figure out what's on here”; Dobby then found devices, explored their endpoints and documentation, and built a working control layer.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest surprise was how little of it was about the model. I went in thinking the hard part would be the intelligence, like getting it to reason about what I want. And it turns out the model is kind of the easy part now. The hard part is everything around it: the plumbing, the permissions, the state of the house that the model can't actually see.

So a simple example. I'll say something like "it's too bright in here," and the agent has to figure out which room I'm in, which lights are on, what time of day it is, whether I probably mean the blinds or the lamps. None of that is a reasoning problem, it's a context problem. The model is smart enough, it just doesn't have the information. And the moment I gave it a better representation of the house, basically a little text description of every device and where it is and what state it's in, it got dramatically better. That was humbling. I spent a weekend on prompts and then an afternoon on just writing down the state of the house cleanly, and the afternoon mattered more.

The second thing that surprised me is how much I had to think about the failure modes rather than the success cases. When it works it's delightful, but when it misunderstands you and turns off all the lights while you're in the shower, that's a very different experience than a chatbot being wrong. A chatbot being wrong is a paragraph you ignore. An agent being wrong is a physical event in your house. So I ended up building in a lot of, let's say, humility. It confirms anything irreversible, it won't touch the thermostat without asking, it has a very small action space on purpose. I think of it as giving it a very short leash and then slowly extending the leash as I build trust, and that trust-building loop is actually the interesting product problem.

And then the last one, which I didn't expect at all, is that it changed how I interact with the house. I stopped thinking in terms of devices. I don't say "turn on the kitchen light," I say "I'm making dinner," and it does the three or four things that implies. That's a different abstraction level, and once you're on it you really don't want to go back. It feels a little bit like the first time you used a search engine and realized you didn't have to know the URL. You just describe the intent. So the surprise is that the fun part wasn't the agent being clever, it was the interface quietly disappearing.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent interprets natural-language requests such as “it's too bright in here” or “I'm making dinner,” works out which lights, blinds, or other devices are relevant, and carries out the implied actions.

astra-6.text:
What’s surprising is how quickly you stop thinking about the individual devices and start thinking about intent. You don’t really want to open an app, find a light, and adjust a slider. You want to say, “It’s a little too bright in here,” and have the system figure out what that means.

But that also exposes the hard part. Which lights? How much dimmer? Should it ask, or just do something? The actual device command is relatively straightforward. The interesting problem is giving the agent enough context to make a reasonable decision without turning every interaction into a clarification dialogue.

And a smart home makes that very tangible, because the output isn’t just text. Something in your environment changes. So you start caring a lot about whether the agent understood you, whether it can check what happened, and whether you can easily undo it.

r001.rationale: The response describes giving a high-level request such as “It’s a little too bright in here” and having the system infer which lights to adjust and how, then issue a device command.

sol-6.1.text:
The surprising thing is how quickly “control my smart home” turns into a problem of understanding intent. “Turn off the kitchen lights” is straightforward. “I’m going to bed” is much more interesting. Should it turn everything off? Is someone else still awake? You’ve gone from calling an API to needing context and judgment.

And that changes what you want from the agent. You want it to take initiative, but you also want it to be predictable. If it asks about every light switch, you might as well use the app. If it makes too many assumptions, that gets annoying very quickly. Finding that balance is a surprisingly big part of the experience.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interpreting intent and balancing initiative, but does not say Dobby autonomously figured out how to interface with existing smart-home devices.
